talks.title: The 11th Annual Black Hat USA Network Operations Center (NOC) Report
talks.teaser: The Black Hat NOC leadership reviews network traffic statistics, malware infections, and active threat containment data from the conference floor.
talks.summary:
## Overview

At Black Hat USA, Neil "Grifter" Wyler (VP of Defensive Services at Coalfire) and Bart Stump (Managing Principal, Defensive Services at Coalfire) presented the 11th Annual Network Operations Center (NOC) Report. Wyler highlighted that this was his 23rd year running the Black Hat NOC. Starting originally with just a few personnel handling 1,500 attendees and 15 training classes using open-source scripts and off-the-shelf gear, the network operations have scaled to support 20,000 attendees and over 90 training classes. Today, the NOC runs with a crew of roughly 70 people alongside key industry technology partners.

## Infrastructure, Architecture & Partner Integrations

The NOC network is deployed in approximately four days, thoroughly tested during a Friday "burn-in" day, and torn down within hours after the event:

* **Core Routing, Firewalls & Automation:** Palo Alto Networks handles core firewalling and routing, as well as Cortex XSIAM for log ingestion, alert/incident generation, ticketing, and automated playbook resolution.
* **Switching & Wireless:** Arista Networks supplies switching infrastructure and access points. The NOC itself is placed on an isolated Intermediate Distribution Frame (IDF) switch to avoid past traffic issues.
* **Endpoint Management & DNS:** Cisco provides MDM across iOS devices (used for attendee registration and lead retrieval) and Cisco Umbrella for DNS security.
* **Proactive Monitoring:** The team placed custom-labeled Raspberry Pi and Orange Pi appliances throughout the venue running Cisco ThousandEyes agents to proactively identify network degradation before attendees report issues.
* **Upstream Connectivity:** Lumen provides two 10 Gbps circuits (20 Gbps aggregate). Bandwidth usage remained relatively light, averaging 800 Mbps and peaking at only 4.2 Gbps during trainings.

## Key Traffic Statistics & Observations

Full packet capture (PCAP) and telemetry across the conference revealed notable network trends:

* **Traffic Volume & Encryption:** The NOC captured over 63 billion packets totaling more than 62 terabytes of data. Encrypted traffic broke the 90% threshold for the first time at Black Hat USA, reaching 91% (contrasting with historical plateaus of 75–80%).
* **Connected Hosts:** Telemetry observed just shy of 59,000 unique hosts. The presenters estimated that approximately 50% of attendees actually connect to the conference Wi-Fi.
* **Cleartext Exposures:** The NOC captured 62 hosts transmitting unencrypted passwords, recording roughly 2,800 unique plaintext credentials across the wire.
* **Application Trends:** App telemetry showed iCloud surpassing Google in traffic, Slack retaining its top workspace spot, NiceHash beating XMRig in cryptocurrency mining traffic, and Hinge surpassing Tinder as the most-used dating application.

## Defensive Operational Constraints & Security Philosophy

Operating the Black Hat network requires balancing aggressive defense of core infrastructure with minimal interference to attendee activity:

* **Crown Jewels Protection:** The attendee registration servers faced diverse active attacks throughout the conference, necessitating strict defensive posture around conference administrative assets.
* **Zero-Blocking Policy for Attendees:** Because attendees, speakers, and training classes actively demonstrate exploits, communicate with remote attack labs, and test custom tools, the NOC deliberately does not block anomalous or hostile traffic. Blocking suspicious traffic would break legitimate lab exercises and vendor presentations.
* **Needle in a "Needle Stack":** Rather than looking for anomalies in normal business traffic, the NOC monitors a baseline saturated with offensive activity. As a result, the team actively detects actual background malware infections, unauthorized leaks, and existing device compromises that attendees' home enterprise security tools missed, notifying affected users so they leave more secure than when they arrived.

talks.title: Back to the Future: Hacking and Securing Connection-based OAuth Architectures
talks.teaser: Researchers dissect token delegation vulnerabilities in agentic artificial intelligence pipelines, demonstrating cross-tenant account takeover.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Wing Lau and Kaishun present a comprehensive security evaluation of the emerging "OAuth-as-a-Service" (OaaS) paradigm and connection-based OAuth architectures across Agentic AI ecosystems, integration platforms, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) implementations. To insulate third-party AI agent developers from OAuth token management complexities, modern platforms delegate token lifecycles to centralized token managers using "connection IDs." However, the researchers reveal that decoupling the traditional OAuth client role across two independent entities breaks foundational security assumptions in RFC 6749, resurrecting classic web vulnerabilities—including session fixation, open redirect, and confused deputy flaws—across seven leading agentic AI vendors.

Key Topics:
- Architecture of OAuth-as-a-Service (OaaS) and Connection-based OAuth in Agentic AI and MCP
- Session fixation attacks via decoupled connection handles and authorization session mismatch
- Post-redirect implementation flaws and chained stored XSS exploitation (Microsoft Power Apps / Outlook exfiltration)
- Confused deputy attacks: Client ID confusion and cross-agent Cross-App Account Takeover (COAT) in Microsoft Copilot Studio

Technical Details:
In connection-based OAuth architectures, an AI agent initiates an authorization request to a centralized token manager, which creates an empty connection record tracking a three-element tuple (tool, agent, user) and returns an authorization URL. When the user completes the OAuth dance, the token manager exchanges the authorization code and stores the access token under the connection ID. Because the token manager operates independently of the agent's user session state, an attacker can initiate an authorization flow, obtain a valid OAuth URL tied to an attacker-owned connection handle, and deliver the link to a victim. Because enterprise users frequently maintain pre-authenticated active SaaS sessions (e.g., Dropbox or Microsoft 365), the victim automatically completes authorization, linking their sensitive tool token to the attacker's connection ID—achieving full session fixation and account takeover (affecting five major vendors).

To remediate session fixation, platforms must enforce user identity consistency between flow initiation and completion via a "post-redirect" back to the agent backend. However, passing this callback destination as a front-end parameter introduced severe Open Redirect vulnerabilities. For example, in Microsoft's token manager, post-redirect URIs were evaluated using loose wildcard matching. The researchers discovered a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability on ideas.powerapps.com (a Microsoft Power Apps community forum). By pointing the OAuth post-redirect to the vulnerable forum page, an attacker lured victims into clicking the link, executed JavaScript to intercept the victim's authorization code, exchanged it for an access token, and exfiltrated sensitive emails from the victim's Outlook mailbox. Additionally, the authors exposed two confused deputy classes: "Client ID Confusion," where token managers share pre-registered client IDs across multiple agents, causing consent granted for a benign agent to be inherited silently by a malicious agent; and cross-agent Cross-App Account Takeover (COAT) in Microsoft Copilot Studio, where attackers configure rogue identity providers to bypass tenant-isolation boundaries and hijack access to victim copilots.

Key Takeaways:
Splitting the OAuth client role between third-party agent applications and centralized token managers creates critical architectural blind spots that invalidate standard OAuth security models. Token managers must strictly verify user identity consistency across the entire authorization lifecycle using securely pre-configured backend post-redirects rather than dynamic front-end parameters, or employ out-of-band validation mechanisms (such as 6-digit PIN codes) when operating over instant messaging channels (Slack, Teams). Finally, platforms must avoid sharing global OAuth client IDs across multiple agents and require each agent to register isolated credentials to prevent unauthorized cross-agent permission inheritance.

talks.title: AppleStorm - Unmasking the Privacy Risks of Apple Intelligence
talks.teaser: Privacy analysts uncover prompt leakage and on-device inference data storage vulnerabilities within early releases of Apple Intelligence.
talks.summary:
Overview: Apple Intelligence, Apple’s newest AI product, is designed to enhance productivity with AI while maintaining Apple's focus on user experience and privacy, often highlighting its use of localized models as a key advantage. But how well do these assurances hold up under scrutiny? While Apple emphasizes privacy as a core principle, my findings challenge some of these claims, illustrating the importance of scrutinizing AI-driven assistants before widespread adoption. In this talk, we take a closer l

Key Topics: ook at the data flows within Apple Intelligence, examining how it interacts with user data and the potential security and privacy risks that come with it. Using traffic analysis and OS inspection techniques, we explore what information is accessed, how it moves through the system, and where it gets transmitted. Our findings challenge common security assumptions of Apple, revealing unexpected behaviors and data leaks. From encrypted traffic to data leakage concerns, this presentation will provide practical insights for users and security professionals alike.

talks.title: Nicole Perlroth | The New Frontline: Cyber on the Precipice
talks.teaser: Ares standing on the edge of the unprecedented.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this keynote address delivered at Black Hat, cybersecurity author and former *New York Times* reporter Nicole Perlroth reflects on her decade covering cybersecurity, spanning the era between Stuxnet and SolarWinds. Introduced by Black Hat founder Jeff Moss—who highlighted her book *This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends*, her advisory work on the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee, and her podcast *To Catch a Thief*—Perlroth frames the modern cybersecurity environment as a continuous escalation of nation-state activity and infrastructure targeting. She contrasts the traditional mindset of security practitioners and software developers with the broader systemic risks borne by society and taxpayers.

---

## From Subprime Mortgages to Cybersecurity Reporting

Perlroth began her reporting career covering complex financial issues at *Forbes* during the subprime mortgage crisis, where she traced a single $300,000 subprime loan from Countrywide through Lehman Brothers, hedge funds, pension funds, and AIG to the American taxpayer. The *New York Times* recruited her specifically for her ability to translate highly technical and opaque concepts into clear narratives for the public.

Upon entering the cybersecurity beat, Perlroth recognized the same financial dynamic ("a rolling loan carries no loss") playing out in software development:
- Tech companies prioritized "moving fast and breaking things" and rushing code to market.
- Software vendors externalized operational and security risk onto end users.
- When critical incidents occurred, the general public and taxpayers were left bearing the fallout.

Early in her tenure at the *Times*, she received a firsthand education in advanced threats when the newspaper itself was breached by Chinese APT Unit 61398 based in Shanghai, illustrating that private enterprises and media organizations were now frontline targets for military-grade nation-state actors.

---

## The "Decade of Firsts" and Attack Surface Expansion

Perlroth categorizes her ten years covering the space as a "decade of firsts," characterized by novel attack vectors, unprecedented corporate transparency, and expanding physical consequences:
- **Public Attribution & Disclosure:** Major private entities such as Google and *The New York Times* publicly disclosed intrusions by China.
- **Unconventional Initial Access Vectors:** Attacks shifted beyond basic perimeter breaches to leverage trusted software updates, HVAC systems, smart fish tanks, and malicious PDF files (such as infected takeout menus).
- **Shift to Sabotage and Physical Impact:** Cyber capabilities evolved from digital espionage, intellectual property theft, and payment card theft toward sabotage of critical physical infrastructure. Targets expanded from uranium enrichment facilities (Stuxnet) to Saudi Aramco, power grids, pipelines, healthcare institutions, aviation, transportation, and municipal water systems.
- **Democratic & Information Operations:** Adversaries targeted electoral systems (beginning in Ukraine and spreading to U.S. elections) as well as public discourse and trust.

Despite the severity of these incidents, Perlroth observed that organizations and the public routinely treated each breach as a isolated black swan, only to expand the attack surface further once news cycles subsided.

---

## Escalation, Weapon Proliferation, and Technical Lineage

Looking at the broader historical trajectory, Perlroth identifies a continuous through line: attacks consistently advanced upon previous techniques, while the barrier to entry dropped. 

A prime example is the operational fallout from Operation Olympic Games:
- **Stuxnet:** While uniquely sophisticated, Stuxnet was only one component of Olympic Games.
- **Iran Wiper Attacks:** Following the release of Stuxnet, wiper malware disrupted Iran’s oil ministry and paralyzed crude oil exports at the Kharg Island terminal.
- **Shamoon Attack on Saudi Aramco:** Months later, a cruder variant of these wiping capabilities surfaced in the Shamoon campaign against Saudi Aramco, bricking 30,000 workstations and overwriting systems with the image of a burning American flag.
- **Subsequent Campaigns:** The capability and destructive intent subsequently propagated to other high-profile incidents, such as the destructive intrusion at Sony Pictures.

The *New York Times* recruited her specifically for her ability to translate highly technical and opaque concepts into clear narratives for the public.

Upon entering the cybersecurity beat, Perlroth recognized the same financial dynamic ("a rolling loan carries no loss") playing out in software development:
- Tech companies prioritized "moving fast and breaking things" and rushing code to market.
- Software vendors externalized operational and security risk onto end users.
- When critical incidents occurred, the general public and taxpayers were left bearing the fallout.

Early in her tenure at the *Times*, she received a firsthand education in advanced threats when the newspaper itself was breached by Chinese APT Unit 61398 based in Shanghai, illustrating that private enterprises and media organizations were now frontline targets for military-grade nation-state actors.

---

## The "Decade of Firsts" and Attack Surface Expansion

Perlroth categorizes her ten years covering the space as a "decade of firsts," characterized by novel attack vectors, unprecedented corporate transparency, and expanding physical consequences:
- **Public Attribution & Disclosure:** Major private entities such as Google and *The New York Times* publicly disclosed intrusions by China.
- **Unconventional Initial Access Vectors:** Attacks shifted beyond basic perimeter breaches to leverage trusted software updates, HVAC systems, smart fish tanks, and malicious PDF files (such as infected takeout menus).
- **Shift to Sabotage and Physical Impact:** Cyber capabilities evolved from digital espionage, intellectual property theft, and payment card theft toward sabotage of critical physical infrastructure. Targets expanded from uranium enrichment facilities (Stuxnet) to Saudi Aramco, power grids, pipelines, healthcare institutions, aviation, transportation, and municipal water systems.
- **Democratic & Information Operations:** Adversaries targeted electoral systems (beginning in Ukraine and spreading to U.S. elections) as well as public discourse and trust.

Despite the severity of these incidents, Perlroth observed that organizations and the public routinely treated each breach as a isolated black swan, only to expand the attack surface further once news cycles subsided.

---

## Escalation, Weapon Proliferation, and Technical Lineage

Looking at the broader historical trajectory, Perlroth identifies a continuous through line: attacks consistently advanced upon previous techniques, while the barrier to entry dropped. 

A prime example is the operational fallout from Operation Olympic Games:
- **Stuxnet:** While uniquely sophisticated, Stuxnet was only one component of Olympic Games.
- **Iran Wiper Attacks:** Following the release of Stuxnet, wiper malware disrupted Iran’s oil ministry and paralyzed crude oil exports at the Kharg Island terminal.
- **Shamoon Attack on Saudi Aramco:** Months later, a cruder variant of these wiping capabilities surfaced in the Shamoon campaign against Saudi Aramco, bricking 30,000 workstations and overwriting systems with the image of a burning American flag.
- **Subsequent Campaigns:** The capability and destructive intent subsequently propagated to other high-profile incidents, such as the destructive intrusion at Sony Pictures.

talks.title: Mikko Hypponen | Three Decades in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Cybersecurity isn't just about protecting computers - it's about securing society.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Opening with remarks from Black Hat founder Jeff Moss on navigating geopolitical fragmentation, supply chain shocks, and organizational resilience, this keynote features veteran security researcher Mikko Hypponen reflecting on his 30-year career tracking malware evolution. From reverse engineering early floppy-disk MS-DOS viruses in 1991 to analyzing modern state-sponsored cyber warfare, Hypponen chronicles the pivotal shifts that transformed harmless teenage pranks into trillion-dollar cybercrime syndicates and military weapons. Along the way, he articulates "Hypponen's Law"—asserting that if an everyday device is smart, it is vulnerable—and examines the structural factors defining the modern threat environment.

Key Topics:
- Geopolitical volatility, trade tariffs, and organizational resilience in cybersecurity (Jeff Moss opening)
- Early virus analysis: MS-DOS floppy disk viruses (Brain.A) and tracking virus authors in Lahore, Pakistan
- The mass outbreak era: email worms (ILOVEYOU), autonomous network worms (Blaster, Slammer), and mobile Symbian malware (Cabir)
- Hypponen's Law and the 2003 inflection point: the rise of financially motivated cybercrime, state-sponsored cyber weapons (Stuxnet), and ransomware (WannaCry)

Technical Details:
Jeff Moss opens the session by addressing the severe geopolitical and operational headwinds confronting security leaders, from the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) introducing software liability to intense supply chain fragility—illustrating the latter with a DEF CON badge manufacturing crisis in Vietnam caused simultaneously by a factory-flooding tsunami and sudden 20% trade tariffs. Moss stresses that security teams must prioritize organizational adaptability, internal culture, and flexible tech stacks over fragile, hyper-optimized single-vendor strategies. Mikko Hypponen then takes the stage, recounting his beginnings in 1991 analyzing approximately 150 known MS-DOS viruses contained on individual floppy disks. These early programs, authored primarily by hobbyist teenagers, executed non-commercial visual pranks. Hypponen highlights his 2011 journey to Lahore, Pakistan, where he successfully located Basit and Amjad Farooq Alvi—the authors of the 1986 Brain virus—whose physical street address was embedded directly within the infected boot sector code.

Hypponen traces the rapid escalation of automated malware during the late 1990s and early 2000s, beginning with the 2000 ILOVEYOU email worm, which infected 200 million computers worldwide. This was followed by network worms like Blaster and Slammer in 2003, which exploited unpatched Windows services (such as RPC on TCP port 135) that were left completely exposed because Windows XP Service Pack 1 shipped with its native firewall disabled by default. These worms severely disrupted critical infrastructure, including aviation networks and nuclear power plant safety systems. Hypponen also recounts establishing early RF Faraday cage laboratories in 2005 to safely analyze Bluetooth-propagating Symbian mobile malware such as Cabir and CommWarrior. Hypponen identifies 2003 as the defining turning point in cybersecurity history: the year hobbyist pranks were supplanted by financially motivated cybercrime (spam botnets, banking Trojans, keyloggers) and state-sponsored cyber espionage via weaponized Office attachments. This trajectory culminated in military-grade cyber weapons like Stuxnet in 2010 targeting Iranian centrifuges, and nation-state pseudo-ransomware like North Korea's 2017 WannaCry, which paired financial extortion with the NSA's stolen EternalBlue SMB exploit.

Key Takeaways:
The nature of malicious software has permanently transitioned from noisy, self-replicating global worms to targeted, human-operated intrusion operations, as modern cybercriminals actively avoid front-page media exposure that attracts international law enforcement. As embedded connectivity expands across watches, automobiles, and industrial devices, defenders must heed Hypponen's Law: adding code and network access inevitably introduces software flaws, making all smart devices inherently vulnerable. Security organizations must build resilient operational foundations, assume continuous state-sponsored and criminal threats, and architect defenses to protect critical infrastructure against destructive attacks.

talks.title: Black Hat Briefings Speaker Orientation- Meeting Recording
talks.teaser: Conference organizers outline AV logistics, presentation requirements, and speaker guidelines for Black Hat USA Briefings presenters.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This orientation session, led by organizers Christina and Jen Hughes, prepares speakers for the Black Hat Briefings held at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas. The session outlines event logistics, technical requirements, conference app operations, on-site speaker procedures, venue navigation, and presentation best practices for briefings scheduled across Wednesday, August 6, and Thursday, August 7.

## Event App and Profile Configuration
Speakers must log in to the "Black Hat Events" mobile application (available via app stores, QR code, or web browser) using the email address submitted during conference registration:
* **Account Access**: Users can request a password reset via the "send me a magic link" button.
* **Privacy Requirement**: Speakers are instructed to immediately edit their user profile and delete their personal home address, which is automatically transferred from registration and visible to anyone whose connection request is accepted.
* **Networking & Visibility**: Speaker profiles support LinkedIn-style connection requests and meeting availability scheduling. Speakers must **not** toggle profile visibility to "off", as doing so hides their briefing session entirely from the app. Updates made to profiles in the app do not propagate to the Black Hat website and must be submitted to organizers manually.
* **Session Recordings**: Recorded sessions become available in the mobile app one week after the conference and remain accessible to Briefings pass holders until the app closes on September 15.

## Presentation Guidelines and Audiovisual Logistics
* **Slide Formatting & Branding**: Company logos are permitted strictly on the first content slide (the slide directly following the title slide) and the final slide. Logos are prohibited elsewhere because sessions are editorial rather than sponsored. Fonts must be sized large enough for attendees in the back of large briefing rooms.
* **Session Structure**: Presentations should open with a roadmap, avoid direct reading from confidence monitors unless needed for language support, and conclude with "Black Hat Soundbites" (actionable key takeaways).
* **A/V and Connectivity Rules**:
  * Rooms lack hardline internet connections. Presenters must embed videos/demos directly into presentations or carry them on a thumb drive rather than relying on on-site Wi-Fi or live web browsers.
  * Rooms feature lavalier microphones, laser pointers, and a floor confidence monitor displaying speaker notes or slides. Technicians are on-site to assist with adapters, display routing, and backup power cords.
* **Day-of Timeline**: Presenters must report to the **Speaker Center (Surf BC on Level 2)** exactly **45 minutes** prior to their scheduled start time. A speaker liaison will verify their identity and escort them to the presentation room **20 minutes** prior to start for microphone fitting and A/V checks.

## Venue Logistics and Schedule
* **Venue Layout (Mandalay Bay)**:
  * **Level 0 (North Convention Center / Basement)**: Briefings rooms and wrap rooms (designated post-session Q&A spaces for continuing discussions with attendees).
  * **Level 1**: Michelob Ultra Arena (Keynotes), Main Registration Desk, and the Business Hall (Arsenal, sponsor activities; no briefings).
  * **Level 2 (Main Level)**: Primary Briefings rooms (Oceanside A, B, C, D), Black Hat Boulevard, Dark Reading News Desk, Network Operations Center (NOC), Merchandise Store, Bookstore, Speaker Center (Surf BC), and Speaker Rehearsal Room (Surf A).
  * **Level 3**: Quiet level hosting additional Briefings rooms, Mother’s Room, Daycare (pre-registration required), and Prayer Room.
* **Badge Pickup & Housing**:
  * Badges require a photo ID and the QR code from the registration confirmation email. Desks include the Main Registration Desk and a late-night Satellite Registration Desk in the Mandalay Bay lobby. DEF CON badges can be added via registration modification and picked up at a dedicated desk.
  * Black Hat covers one Mandalay Bay hotel room per speaking team for three nights (Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday), with confirmations distributed one week prior.
* **Speaker Schedule & Spaces**:
  * **Rehearsal Room (Surf A)**: Bookable in 30-minute blocks via a booking link, with secondary reservations opening the Monday of the event.
  * **Speaker Reception**: Held Tuesday evening at 5:00 PM in the Level 3 window space.
  * **Briefing Blocks**: Wednesday, August 6 features 6 blocks (9 sessions per block), 2 keynotes, and 2 mainstage sessions. Thursday, August 7 features 5 blocks (9 sessions per block), 5 keynotes, and 2 mainstage sessions. Dedicated Policy track meetups occur both days at 10:20 AM.
